title.en: Crystal clues: The case of the Lava Creek Tuff’s missing members
title.vi: Manh mối từ tinh thể: Vụ án những thành viên bị thất lạc của lớp đá trầm tích núi lửa Lava Creek Tuff (*Lava Creek Tuff*) kinh điển (*classic*) trong địa chất học (*geology*) khu vực núi lửa Yellowstone (*Yellowstone*). Cùng tìm hiểu chi tiết về nghiên cứu mới nhất từ các nhà khoa học Montana State University (*Montana State University*) giúp định hình lại hệ thống siêu phun trào (*supereruption*). Khám phá cách các khoáng vật như amphibole (*amphibole*) và sanidine (*sanidine*) tiết lộ sự thật đằng sau mô hình hai thành viên (*two-member framework*) truyền thống đã tồn tại nhiều thập kỷ nay trong giới khoa học và nghiên cứu dung nham (*magma*). Bài viết thuộc chuyên mục Biên niên sử miệng núi lửa Yellowstone (*Yellowstone Caldera Chronicles*) do chuyên gia Stacy Henderson (*Stacy Henderson*) thực hiện giúp mở ra góc nhìn hoàn toàn mới về lịch sử địa chất trái đất (*earth sciences*). Xem ngay tóm tắt và các bước áp dụng thực tế bên dưới để hiểu thêm về phương pháp nghiên cứu hiện đại này nhé! Cập nhật liên tục các thông tin khoa học mới nhất cho bạn đọc yêu thích khám phá thiên nhiên và khoa học Trái Đất (*Earth sciences*). Nội dung được tổng hợp từ nguồn chính thống và uy tín quốc tế dành cho cộng đồng học thuật và những ai quan tâm đến núi lửa học (*volcanology*). Đọc thêm để không bỏ lỡ các phát hiện bất ngờ về lớp trầm tích tro bụi (*ash flow*) cổ đại này nhé bạn ơi! Hãy cùng theo dõi hành trình giải mã bí ẩn địa chất thú vị này ngay nào mọi người ơi! Đừng quên chia sẻ bài viết nếu bạn thấy thú vị và hữu ích nhé bạn của tôi ơi! Chúc bạn có những trải nghiệm đọc sách và nghiên cứu khoa học thật tuyệt vời trên ứng dụng Reader của chúng tôi mỗi ngày nhé bạn ơi! Thân ái và chào quyết thắng nhé bạn của tôi ơi, chúng ta cùng bắt đầu khám phá ngay thôi nào các bạn ơi! hook.en:
*Yellowstone Caldera Chronicles is a weekly column written by scientists and collaborators of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. This week's contribution is from Stacy Henderson, Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Earth Sciences at Montana State University.*

*“The present is the key to the past.”* -- Charles Lyell

sections.body_en: Imagine using the same map for decades, only to discover that one of the lines on it never really existed. That’s essentially what a new study suggests about the Lava Creek Tuff, the deposit left behind by Yellowstone’s 631,000-year-old supereruption.

The Lava Creek Tuff (LCT) is made up of more than 1,000 km³ (240 mi³) of material that was ejected during the formation of Yellowstone Caldera—an eruption that spread ash across much of North America. Since it was initially mapped as an ash flow in the 1960s, the Lava Creek Tuff has been divided into two units known simply as member A and member B. The main distinguishing feature of LCT-A was the presence of the mineral amphibole, which was not found in the rocks of LCT-B. This evidence implied that two different magma bodies fed the eruption, providing important insights for volcanologists as to how melt was situated in the crust prior to these catastrophic events.

For decades, the two-member framework served as the cornerstone for describing and interpreting the Lava Creek Tuff, shaping how scientists understood the eruption and magma system that produced it. However, several recent studies began to uncover Lava Creek Tuff deposits that did not fit neatly into either member A or member B. Recent work has shown that rocks in the Sour Creek dome previously mapped as the 2.1-million-year-old Huckleberry Ridge Tuff are actually part of the Lava Creek eruption, and many of these rocks do not fit neatly into either the member A or member B classification. These findings raise an important question: if some Lava Creek Tuff deposits cannot be classified as either member, is the two-member model still the best way to divide Yellowstone’s most recent supereruption?

To find out, geologists at Montana State University (MSU) started an immense project: a fresh look at the entire Lava Creek Tuff eruption. This required sampling deposits stretching from Warm River, Idaho, to Greybull, Wyoming, as well as climbing up and down canyons, over scree slopes, and sometimes (when they were lucky) flying to the most remote parts of Yellowstone National Park. Researchers focused on mapping amphibole occurrence and comparing deposits to the newly recognized Sour Creek dome units. MSU scientists also analyzed chemical compositions of the mineral sanidine from each sample. These crystals preserve a chemical fingerprint that can test whether the Lava Creek Tuff truly divides into two distinct members.

To start, researchers made thin slices of each of the collected rocks, examining more than 100 samples under the microscope. Despite this extensive search, only 13 amphibole crystals were identified, mostly from a small region near Madison Junction, and three of those crystals came from deposits mapped as member B. This immediately blurs the traditional distinction between the two members. Even more intriguing, half the crystals identified were found within a small deposit along the Gibbon River that turned out to be 140,000 years older than the Lava Creek Tuff eruption. This means one of the key amphibole-rich deposits used to define member A is not part of the Lava Creek Tuff at all.

If amphibole is rare, occurs in both members, and one of the amphibole-rich examples isn’t even LCT, how strong is the two-member framework really?

The next clue came from sanidine crystals. Scientists analyzed the barium content in sanidine from deposits mapped as both members A and B. If the two-member framework reflected a real division within the eruption, the crystal chemistry should match, and there would be two separate populations of crystals. Instead, the sanidine chemistry shows that the same barium chemistry occurs in both mapped members. Essentially, all methods tested failed to find clean division between LCT-A and LCT-B.

So, what does this all mean for the Lava Creek Tuff? The evidence from both amphibole and sanidine chemistry points to the same conclusion: the LCT deposits do not naturally separate into member A and member B. Instead, the LCT appears to record a more complex eruptive story than the traditional two-member framework suggests. Moving forward, scientists will need to rethink how the deposit is divided, draw new lines on the map, and revisit previous interpretations of the eruption and the magmas that produced it.

(These new results were recently published in *Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal* Research, at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvolgeores.2026.108753.)

origin.originalTitle: Crystal clues: The case of the Lava Creek Tuff’s missing members
